text: Lesson 13 showed a dependency crossing a tier boundary and breaking a failover that looked clean on its own. That's the easy version of the problem — one call, one obvious dependency. At real enterprise scale, with dozens of services, nobody can hold the actual dependency graph in their head, which means nobody can correctly answer 'what's really affected if this fails' without something written down and current.

That something is a service catalog: every service with an owner, its RTO and RPO tier, and an explicit list of what it calls and what calls it. The part that actually makes it useful isn't the catalog existing — plenty of outdated architecture diagrams exist — it's keeping it current by discovering real dependencies instead of only trusting what someone documented, and treating blast radius as the full transitive closure of that graph, not just the first hop out.

Documentation drifts the moment someone adds a call under deadline pressure and forgets to update the diagram. Distributed tracing catches what documentation misses: a real trace through checkout shows it calling pricing-service and inventory-service as expected, but also surfaces that inventory-service makes an undocumented synchronous call into a legacy warehouse database nobody flagged as a dependency at all. That's a real coupling, whether or not it was ever written down, and it's exactly the kind of thing that only shows up when you go looking with tracing instead of trusting the wiki.

Once the graph is accurate, blast radius becomes a query instead of a guess. A checkout database failure doesn't just hit checkout — querying the graph surfaces order-history directly, then pricing-service, inventory-service, tax-rules-service, and the legacy warehouse database transitively, plus notifications because it reads order-history. That's the actual set a failover decision has to account for, and it's considerably larger than 'the one service that's obviously down.'

A dependency map that's accurate changes what a failover decision looks like, but someone still has to act on it fast enough to matter. Next, why that someone probably shouldn't be a human reading a runbook at three in the morning — and what automating failover against health checks and runbook-as-code actually buys you instead.
